Markowsky Parabola

GeometryCurvesConstructions
Game: Move two dots on a curve and watch two angles at D that always match.
How to play: Drag A or B along the curve, or use the sliders. Tick the boxes to show names, angle numbers or extra lines; press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

Two dots on a curve, one line through the vertex and a short horizontal segment: the two turns at D match every time. Move the dots and watch the readings.

Put the curve in coordinates

Let the vertex O be (0, 0) and the axis vertical. A parabola here is y = x²/(4a), with the applet's a = 40. Write the offsets of A and B from the axis as p and q. The line OB has slope q/(4a), so where it crosses the vertical through A it has height pq/(4a). That crossing is C, and D sits on the axis at the same height, so DC is horizontal.

Why the two angles match

From D, the steps to A and B are (p, p(p−q)/(4a)) and (q, q(q−p)/(4a)). Their slopes are (p−q)/(4a) and (q−p)/(4a): the same size with opposite signs. A horizontal ray therefore sees them at equal turns, which is the page's claim ∠ADC = ∠BDC. In other words, DC is the angle bisector of ∠ADB. The logic test checked all 33,670 pairs 0 < p < q ≤ 260 on the exact curve: the largest difference was about 3 × 10−12 degrees, which is rounding in the arithmetic, not a real gap.

What the extra lines are for

At offset t the tangent has slope t/(2a). The tangents at A and B meet at M = ((p+q)/2, pq/(4a)); the line OA meets the vertical through B at K = (q, pq/(4a)). So D, C, K and M are all level. This is the applet's "extra" hint. It is a different question from Markowsky2 ("Three Points on a Parabola"), which uses three dots and asks where the three pairwise tangent intersections lie.

Screen pixels and the stated domain

The applet rounds every curve height to a whole pixel ((t²/4)/a with integer division). The test found that the two drawn readings can differ by up to about 4.2° for very close dots (p = 12, q = 18), but by under 0.1° at the starting offsets. The theorem is about the exact curve. The page's description line says "ADO and BDE"; its body and the applet's angle marks say ADC and BDC, so this page follows those. The equality also needs both dots to the right of the axis, with A nearer O, as the page states.

Tick "Show statement", keep A still and slide B: the two numbers move together. Then tick "Extra" and find M on the horizontal line through D.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
